title: Treating foot rot in sheep
subtitle: Foot rot smells unmistakably. Once you know it, you do not mistake it for anything else.
excerpt: Foot rot is a bacterial infection between the hoof horn and the sole, caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum and Dichelobacter nodosus working together. It is highly contagious and spreads rapidly through a flock in wet conditions. Early cases respond well to antibiotic spray and foot bathing. Established cases need injection. Here is how to recognise the stages and treat each one.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Better Returns Programme, Hoof Health guide. DEFRA Codes of Recommendations for the Welfare of Sheep. SAC Consulting, sheep flock health planning guidance. NADIS (National Animal Disease Information Service) foot rot advisory notes.

glossaryTerms.definition: A contagious bacterial infection of sheep hooves caused by Fusobacterium necrophorum and Dichelobacter nodosus. Produces a characteristic foul smell, separation of the horn from the sole, and severe lameness. Spreads through wet pasture.
Walking sheep through a shallow trough of zinc sulphate or formalin solution to treat and prevent hoof infections. The recommended preventative for foot rot in high-risk conditions.
A 10% zinc sulphate solution used in foot baths to harden hoof horn and reduce bacterial load on the feet. The preferred foot bath chemical for foot rot prevention and mild treatment.

content.text: A sheep with
foot rot

is lame, usually on one front foot. The smell when you turn the hoof over, sweet, rotten, distinct, confirms the diagnosis before you look at the horn. The infection spreads through the flock through wet pasture within days if the lame animal is not removed from the group and treated.
Staging the infection
Stage 1, Foot scald: redness and softening of the skin between the claws. No horn involvement. Spray with antibiotic spray; foot bath for prevention.
Stage 2, Early foot rot: horn beginning to lift at the heel. Strong smell. Antibiotic spray and consider injection if several feet involved.
Stage 3, Established foot rot: horn significantly lifted, black necrotic tissue visible. Injection required; foot bath supportive.
Stage 4, Severe: horn largely detached, deep tissue involved. Vet call, may need systemic antibiotics and possible culling decision.
Treating stages 1-2
Catch and turn the sheep onto its rump. Examine all four feet.
With hoof shears, trim any flap of loosened horn so the sole is open to air and the spray reaches the tissue beneath.
Apply antibiotic oxytetracycline spray liberally to the cleaned foot.
Move the treated animal to a dry, clean area away from the infected pasture.
Foot bathing the rest of the flock
Walk the whole flock through a
foot bath
containing a 10%
zinc sulphate solution

. The trough should be long enough for each sheep to stand in the solution for at least 30 seconds, a 3 m trough with a slow-moving flock achieves this without counting. Repeat every 5-7 days during a wet period.
Injecting for established cases

Stage 3 cases need a systemic antibiotic injection to reach the infection deep in the hoof. Penicillin-streptomycin combination or long-acting oxytetracycline are typical choices. The dose and withdrawal period are on the product label; dose to the sheep's current liveweight, not an estimate. A sheep that does not respond to two injections 5 days apart needs a vet assessment.
